extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in politics, technology policy, and government transparency
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying indicators, data patterns, and procedural weaknesses that reveal fraudulent or inauthentic submissions to government notice-and-comment dockets (case study: FCC net neutrality). Useful for journalists, investigators, and policymakers assessing comment integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap with known data breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: High proportion of commenter email addresses (or other contact data) match records from a known data breach (e.g., 94% overlap with the Modern Business Solutions breach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run bulk email/address lists through breach-identification services (Have I Been Pwned). A very high match rate to a single breach — especially when other submitters do not show similar overlap — is a strong indicator the data were harvested, not voluntarily supplied by commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmically generated / templated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers of comments are iterations of the same template generated by a computer, with only certain words altered (e.g., 1.3 million comments that clustered to the same ungrammatical template).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clustering/text-duplication analysis to detect near-duplicate or templated text. Identical phrasing, repeated ungrammatical constructions, or one-sentence templates repeated with minor substitutions are red flags for automated or mass-produced submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulk upload traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments submitted via bulk-upload mechanisms (e.g., Box.com uploads to the FCC docket) can be traced to the uploader and reveal which organization submitted large batches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request bulk-upload files and metadata (via FOIA where applicable) to identify uploaders. Presence of a common uploader account across suspect batches implicates that organization even if commenter contact fields vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deceased people's names
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments attributed to individuals who are dead (e.g., a person who died more than a year before a comment was posted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check commenter names and birth/death records; appearance of deceased individuals indicates identity misuse or fabrication and is strong evidence of impersonation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional characters and celebrities appearing as commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions attributed to fictional characters (e.g., Boba Fett, Luke Skywalker) or public figures (e.g., 'Barack Obama') using contact data that match other suspicious patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of obviously fake or celebrity names in comment lists signals low-quality/fraudulent data; combine with other indicators (breach overlap, duplicated text) to assess severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsensical or improbable address data
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact fields contain implausible or malformed entries (nonsensical street-and-city combinations, underscores used instead of spaces, or other odd formatting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot-check addresses for validity. Repeated weird formatting across many records suggests automated data-generation or careless data harvesting rather than genuine opt-in submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual email domains and disposable-address patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers of comments use suspicious email domains (e.g., @pornhub.com) or disposable/temporary email addresses (e.g., FakeMailGenerator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag comments using temporary or unusual domains as lower-confidence. While not definitive proof of fraud, paired with other anomalies they strengthen the case for automated or inauthentic submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: High incidence of exact duplicate submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comments are literal duplicates of the same submission (full duplicates), not just similar templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduplicate comment bodies and contact combos to quantify unique submissions versus exact clones; a large number of exact duplicates suggests programmatic reposting rather than individual engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated reuse of the same names/addresses across different campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The same set of names and street addresses appears across unrelated campaigns or dockets (e.g., 99.9% of 100,000 names reappearing a year later on a different issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track overlap of commenter identity lists between campaigns; improbably high reuse indicates a recycled database being repurposed rather than fresh, issue-specific outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: IP-address anomalies and geographic mismatches
rubrics_metrics.description: IP addresses tied to commenters are inconsistent with claimed locations (e.g., Texans signing from IP ranges owned by MLB Advanced Media in New York) or otherwise implausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze IP ranges for geographic plausibility and hosting-provider ownership. Clusters of IPs from unrelated corporate ranges or from centralized infrastructure point to proxying, automation, or server-side posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnatural timestamp distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment timestamps are uniformly distributed across all hours (e.g., equally likely at 3 a.m. as 3 p.m.), contrary to normal human online activity patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot activity by hour/day; non-human patterns (flat distributions, bursts at machine-regular intervals) suggest automated processes or scripted signups rather than organic public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor/submitter history and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Background of firms or individuals involved (e.g., false biographical claims, prior legal testimony alleging fraud) can indicate higher risk of misconduct in comment campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vet vendors: check litigation history, public claims, past allegations, and sworn depositions. Prior findings of fabricated data or deceptive practices increase the plausibility that current submissions are inauthentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrepancy between claimed validation practices and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendors or clients may assert they required name/address/email/phone verification or used 'extensive data validation,' yet the submission patterns (breach overlap, duplicates) contradict effective validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require documentation of validation methods and sample audits. Claims of validation should be corroborated by independent checks (e.g., sampling and contacting supposed signers, cross-referencing against opt-in records).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency procedural vulnerabilities (bulk-upload, no removal mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency practices can enable or fail to mitigate fraud: allowing bulk uploads without transparency, lacking mechanisms to remove fraudulent comments, or not responding substantively to investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess agency policies (bulk-upload acceptance, server-log retention, comment-removal procedures). Reform options include stricter upload controls, better logging, and clear remediation channels for impersonation victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume-based leverage vs. substantive weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Although officials say substance matters more than quantity, published tallies and the optics of large numbers can be exploited to amplify influence even when comments lack substantive, individual input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between counting raw submissions and evaluating substantive, unique contributions. Policymakers and platforms should prioritize qualitative analysis and deweight suspect mass submissions in public tallies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of breached/stolen personal data versus genuine opt-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment lists assembled from purchased or hacked personal-information datasets (stolen identities) differ from lists of consenting individuals who were directly solicited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare submission lists to known breach datasets and to expected patterns from legitimate outreach (e.g., opt-in confirmations, conversion timestamps tied to ad clicks). High correspondence with stolen-data caches indicates identity misuse rather than consented advocacy.
